description: Cosmic Detective is my solo project to reveal how the sky changes through NASA's SPHEREx observations. I'm building an interactive observatory that connects immersive 3D exploration, image comparisons across time and traceable scientific evidence. My goal is to make complex astronomical data accessible through a visually striking, scientifically rigorous experience where anyone can explore the sky, investigate change and understand the evidence behind each finding.
summary:
Pluto was found by comparing two photos of the sky and noticing that one dot had moved. Cosmic Detective brings that moment to anyone, using real images from NASA's SPHEREx mission.

Pick one of the challenge's test targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or type sky coordinates. The SPHEREx images of that patch play like a short video, so a moving star or asteroid catches the eye at once. Compare flips between two dates, and Subtract removes the unchanging sky so that only the change remains. The measured motion appears beside the prediction: Epsilon Indi B moved 6.27″ ± 0.20″ in 505 days, and Gaia predicts 6.31″.

Before a result is shown, the tool checks the images behind it: wavelength, pixel quality flags and alignment, plus the shape of the star (PSF). When the images cannot carry a measurement, it says INCONCLUSIVE and gives the reason in plain words.

Seven fields are prepared in advance and open in seconds. On these you can also browse the sky in 100 of SPHEREx's 102 infrared channels, read spectra, overlay Gaia and WISE, and follow a machine-learning rank of which candidates to inspect first. Any other coordinate goes to NASA's archive as a live query, and when the archive does not answer the site says so and points to the nearest prepared field.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, more than professionals alone can review. Our goal is to turn curious people into careful sky detectives.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The infrared sky is changing. Cosmic Detective lets anyone follow the evidence.

Cosmic Detective is a public web tool built on real images from NASA's SPHEREx, the infrared space telescope launched in March 2025 that maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours. Visitors watch a star or asteroid move, compare the measured motion with the official prediction, and open the observations behind every number.

Who it is for: students, teachers and curious members of the public who want to see real space data change in front of them, and astronomers who want to check how each number was made. Both read the same screen at different depths.

As the challenge notes, volunteers comparing sky images over time have already found many brown dwarfs and comets, for example through Backyard Worlds. Cosmic Detective brings the same method to SPHEREx, whose new all-sky maps arrive every six months.

Headline result: from a shift of about one SPHEREx pixel, the tool measured that Epsilon Indi B moved 6.27″ ± 0.20″ in 505 days. ESA's Gaia catalogue predicts 6.31″.

How to read the numbers: motion on the sky is measured in arcseconds (″). One arcsecond is 1/3600 of a degree, roughly the width of a coin seen from 5 km away.

The experience follows five steps: choose, watch, measure, check, and keep the evidence.

  1. Choose your part of the sky. Start with any of the five challenge targets on the first screen, or enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec). The page link stores the target, viewing mode and selected images, so any view can be shared.
  2. Make change visible. Play runs the images like a short video, and Compare blinks between two observation dates. Under More, Subtract removes the unchanging sky so only what changed remains. On the asteroid fields, Reveal change dims everything that stayed still.
  3. Measure the motion. The tool places the measured motion directly beside the prediction. Epsilon Indi B, a pair of nearby brown dwarfs, moved 6.27″ ± 0.20″ in 505 days; ESA's Gaia star catalogue (DR3) predicts 6.31″. Asteroid 2 Pallas moved 912.18″ ± 0.27″ in 1.77 days; its JPL orbit prediction is 912.27″.
  4. Check what the images support. A status dot on the image opens Match Lock, the tool's comparison check. It looks at three things: the wavelength at which SPHEREx saw the target, whether the target's pixels are flagged as faulty, and whether the images line up on a common sky grid. It then states what the images are good for: watching, subtraction, measuring motion, measuring brightness. On the prepared fields, a shape check compares the source with the model of a single point of light that comes with each SPHEREx image (its ePSF), to tell whether it is one source or a blend. The sky background is compared with the model of zodiacal light, sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust, supplied in the same file.
  5. Keep the evidence. The Evidence button builds an Evidence Pack listing each observation ID, date, wavelength, archive file and processing step. A link reopens the same view, keeping the visual result connected to the observations and processing behind it.

WHAT ELSE IS INSIDE

The seven prepared fields offer additional ways to explore the observations.

  • Colours — the same sky across infrared wavelengths. Under More, Colours shows the same patch of sky in 100 of SPHEREx's 102 wavelength channels, using the DR1 All-Sky Cube. Channels 51 and 52 are empty in that product and are shown as missing rather than as zero. Colours is for looking; every measurement uses the individual images.
  • Spectra — brightness across wavelength. Spectra are built from individual exposures for three fields. For Epsilon Indi B, the result is checked against the official Spectrophotometry Tool of IRSA, NASA's infrared science archive. Across the 109 observations that allow a like-for-like comparison, Cosmic Detective's flux is 1.028 times the tool's (median). The values are the total light inside a fixed circle, without the standard correction for light falling outside it.
  • Time trail — motion through time. The measured positions of an asteroid are displayed with time as the third axis. That axis is labelled as time, not distance.
  • AI rank — a starting point for inspection. On the two asteroid fields, an unsupervised anomaly-detection algorithm (Isolation Forest) orders change candidates by how unusual they are. Without being given the asteroid's position, it placed the known asteroid first in both fields: 2 Pallas among 238 candidates, and 3 Juno among 109. These are the same two fields used to develop the method. On a third field kept aside for testing, 16 Psyche appeared as stationary fragments instead of a moving track, and the site shows that outcome beside the ranking. The rank is an order for inspection, never a classification or a discovery.
  • Context — observations connected to astronomical references. The image can overlay known sources from the Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues, and the all-sky view shows bright Hipparcos stars. Additional tools provide SIMBAD name lookup, an Aladin Lite precision view, predicted asteroid positions from IRSA MOST (JPL Horizons), and a WiseView link. The tool also shows frames from NEOSSat, Canada's asteroid-watching satellite, that cover an asteroid's predicted position, with that position marked.

PREPARED FIELDS AND LIVE SEARCH

Seven fields are prepared in advance from the IRSA archive: the five challenge targets and the fields of asteroids 2 Pallas and 3 Juno. Each is labelled CACHED NASA OBSERVATION and opens in a few seconds.

For any other coordinate, Cosmic Detective sends a live query to IRSA. The service returns the first images as soon as they are ready and adds the rest as they arrive. This path was tested with real archive data on our own machine; on 15 November NASA's archive query service was not responding, so it could not yet be confirmed on the public site.

When the archive does not respond, the site explains the problem in plain language and offers the nearest prepared field.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

All five test targets are included. Each is labelled according to what its data supports, and every inconclusive result states its reason.

  • Epsilon Indi B (a pair of nearby brown dwarfs): measured motion agrees with the Gaia prediction within the uncertainty.
  • Barnard's Star (the fastest-moving star in our sky): the star is so bright that it overflows (saturates) the detector in all 358 observations, so the strict result remains INCONCLUSIVE. A separate, clearly labelled measurement from the fainter outer edges of its image, where the detector does not overflow, gives 10.36″ ± 1.5″ in 362 days, compared with 10.34″ predicted by Gaia.
  • RW Aurigae (a young, variable star): observations from three dates at matching wavelength, spanning two data releases, yield a brightness-variation candidate.
  • R Draconis (a pulsating red giant): INCONCLUSIVE, because the star saturates the detector.
  • WISE 0855 (the coldest known brown dwarf): INCONCLUSIVE, because the source is faint and blends with a neighbouring star.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

A blink shows that two pictures differ. Cosmic Detective also checks whether those pictures can be compared at all.

SPHEREx observes a given point in the sky at a different wavelength on each visit. A brightness change therefore counts only when both images saw the source at the same wavelength, and Cosmic Detective checks this before it measures.

Every result carries its own trust label. A first-time visitor can explore what changed, while an astronomer can examine the same screen in depth. A 3D sky globe leads to any target, and every measurement is made on the original scientific image files (FITS).

The creative contribution is the connection between an accessible visual experience and an inspectable scientific result: visitors can follow a change from the image, through the measurement, to the evidence and its limitations.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Frontend: Vite, React, TypeScript, three.js with React Three Fiber, Plotly, and Aladin Lite.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, Photutils, reproject, PyVO, astroquery, NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn.
  • Data and services: SPHEREx DR1 (Data Release 1) and QR3 (Quick Release) data through IRSA, including TAP, Cutout Service, spectral calibration, All-Sky Cube HiPS, and MOST.
  • Hosting: Vercel and Render.

DESIGN DECISIONS AND SCIENTIFIC SCOPE

  • Traceability: every number on the prepared fields traces back to observation IDs, archive files, and processing steps.
  • Plain language: explanations come first, with technical detail one click away. A Reduce motion switch is available under the ⚙ button.
  • New data: DR1 and QR3 are already used side by side, and every comparison across the two releases is labelled.
  • Scope: the tool is built for desktop screens. The spectrum check covers one target, and the machine-learning result is limited to the two fields on which the method was developed.

USE OF AI (Super Intelligence)

We used AI tools to support our work. During the development process, these AI tools provided us with limited technical support, helping us resolve specific issues, answer technical questions, and make improvements to the code. We reviewed and tested every change ourselves. We also used AI tools at certain points to translate from Turkish to English.
